report.executive_summary: Having recomputed every candidate against the written screen, all four packages qualify: quality indices 82-100 clear the floor of 80 and raw defect counts 0-3 sit under the ceiling of 5, so reject_all is idle. On the single shared duty-test basis, measured energy ranks P4 9 kWh, P3 20, P2 33, P1 50; the minimum is unique, so the ID tie-break is idle and the policy selects P4 outright. P4 pairs the lowest energy with the highest quality index (100) and zero defects. Cost, delivery, maintenance and field reliability are unverified for every candidate and cannot move this ranking. Open items below are non-binding questions.
report.figure_caption: Numbers to scale: measured energy per common HVAC duty (P4 9, P3 20, P2 33, P1 50 kWh) with quality and defect flags; bars drawn to true values.

recommendation.rationale: At 9 kWh on the shared duty basis, P4 is the unique lowest-energy qualifier, 11-41 kWh ahead of every rival, and it also posts the highest quality index (100) with zero raw defects; the written policy selects it outright and no tie-break applies. The P2 contingency in the handover notes is recorded but non-binding.

sections.body: Recomputing the screen row by row: P1 (quality 92, defects 3), P2 (82, 1), P3 (98, 2) and P4 (100, 0) all clear both thresholds, so no candidate is disqualified and none is added. The energy column is the sole remaining decision input: P4 9 kWh, P3 20, P2 33, P1 50, each measured on the identical thermal load, operating period and acceptance conditions named in the work order. Because every package faces the same test basis, this ordering is a genuine efficiency result, not a measurement artifact, and no retest or normalization is needed to read it.
sections.heading: Ranked Results and Qualification

sections.body: Inspection of the gaps shows one leader and one laggard: P4 sits 11 kWh under P3, 24 under P2 and 41 under P1. These margins dwarf any plausible retest noise on a fixed duty, so the ranking P4 < P3 < P2 < P1 is stable under any weighting that still respects the written policy. The quality-energy pattern is consistent: the two best-quality packages, P3 (98) and P4 (100), are also the two lowest-energy ones, while P2's quality index of 82 is the field's lowest. Nothing in the trusted table supports any selection other than P4.
sections.heading: Interpreting the Energy Gaps

sections.body: X-factors here are exactly the scope items the supplied facts omit: purchase cost, delivery schedule, maintenance burden and field reliability. They are unverified for all four candidates, so no claim that one package wins on them is supported, and none may move the ranking. Defect counts deserve one note: they are raw counts against a pass/fail ceiling, not graded quality scores, and P4 is the only defect-free package. If the client later weights defect margin, that is a policy change for a future round, not this decision.
sections.heading: X-Factors Beyond the Trusted Table

sections.body: Handover to the next analyst: re-derive eligibility and gaps from the trusted table before trusting any figure pixel, since round one showed correct prose alongside misdrawn charts. Keep the winner's flawless record under retest scrutiny and record one contingency, rule-based and non-binding: if the selected package fails a later retest, the fallback by fewest raw defects is P2 (one defect, 33 kWh), ahead of P3 (two, 20 kWh) and P1 (three, 50 kWh). Carry forward: defect counts are ceilings only; P1's margin is two counts; every cost and reliability item is unverified.
